questions.q: Does replying to reviews improve a restaurant's star rating?
questions.a: Yes, replying consistently is linked to better ratings. Momos's internal analysis of 504 brands' Google review data looked at how reply rate relates to star rating over time. When you reply to more of your reviews, guests see that you're listening, and that tends to show up in your rating.

questions.q: Does a higher star rating actually increase restaurant revenue?
questions.a: It does, according to research by Michael Luca at Harvard Business School, which the post uses to connect ratings with revenue. His work found that a better rating on review sites goes along with higher revenue. So moving your rating up, for example from 3.5 to 4.0, is worth real effort.

questions.q: What is a review reply rate?
questions.a: Your review reply rate is the share of reviews you've responded to in a given period. If you get a hundred reviews in a month and reply to eighty of them, your reply rate is eighty percent. Tracking it by location shows you where replies are falling behind.

questions.q: Should I reply to positive reviews as well as negative ones?
questions.a: Yes, replying to both counts toward your reply rate and shows every guest that you read what they write. A quick, personal thank-you to a happy guest takes little time and encourages them to come back. Negative reviews still deserve priority, because a thoughtful reply can win back an unhappy guest.

questions.q: How can a multi-location restaurant keep up with review replies?
questions.a: Set a clear target for reply rate at every location and check it each month alongside your star rating. Bringing reviews from all your stores into one inbox makes it far easier to spot which locations are falling behind. Many brands use AI to draft on-brand replies so the team only needs to review and approve them.
